overview: This file contains two internal State Department memoranda concerning Japanese electric-power development and American technical or financial connections to it. A November 1940 memorandum records engineering executive Gano Dunn’s decision, endorsed informally by Far Eastern Affairs officials, to decline Mitsui and Company’s request for help constructing hydraulic and steam power plants in Japan because such assistance might advance Japanese policy. A November 1943 memorandum considers whether a 1923 report by the Toho Electric Power Company—originally prepared in anticipation of seeking a United States loan—might be useful to wartime agencies, but records that neither the Military Intelligence Service nor the Office of Economic Warfare wanted it.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Mitsui’s request for American engineering assistance
subfiles.about: Records Gano Dunn’s proposed refusal of Mitsui and Company’s request that the J. G. White Engineering Corporation help plan and erect hydraulic and steam power plants in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Gano Dunn explained that Mitsui and Company had asked his engineering corporation to assist with Japanese hydraulic and steam power projects. Drawing on his experience as a member of the National Defense Commission, Dunn believed that no action should be taken that might further Japan’s current policies and proposed a polite refusal based on his company’s national-defense commitments. Ballantine and Mackay informally approved his proposed course and thanked him for bringing the matter to the Department’s attention.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on possible use of the Toho Electric Power Company report
subfiles.about: Records unsuccessful efforts to identify a wartime government use for a detailed 1923 report on the Toho Electric Power Company.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that J. R. Thomas had sent Stanley K. Hornbeck a copy of the Toho Electric Power Company’s detailed report dated April 30, 1923. The Military Intelligence Service advised that it had no need for the volume. Halleck Butts of the Office of Economic Warfare explained that the publication had been prepared as a preliminary to a United States loan request, that copies were already held in the United States, and that he could identify no interested recipient.

interest: The file illustrates two distinct stages in the contraction of American economic engagement with Japan: a private firm’s voluntary refusal of technical assistance in 1940 and the wartime government’s lack of interest in an older Japanese corporate report in 1943. The Dunn memorandum is especially useful for showing how business leaders consulted the State Department informally and aligned commercial decisions with emerging national-defense policy before the United States entered the war. The later memorandum also reveals how officials evaluated—and sometimes rejected—prewar corporate intelligence that had originally been assembled to attract American financing.
